lines.text: I
The remarkable thing is that Paul illustrates his thesis that
our present existence is provisional and that our true and
fulfilled existence is yet to come, by a consideration of the
world of creatures outside the human sphere: "For the
creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the
sons of God; for the creation was subjected to futility not
of its own will but by the will of him who subjected it in
hope; because the creation itself will be set free from its
bondage to decay, and obtain the glorious liberty of the
children of God."
Even the creatures of the world of nature are not as they
should be. They are filled with a longing for release from
their bondage; against their own will, against what they
truly should and want to be, they were subjected to futility,
i.e. to transience. They cannot freely develop their forces of
life; their freedom of growth is checked and they are
maimed.
What is the meaning of this? Can we understand it? Have
we not here a mythological mode of speech? Still more
mythological is Paul's suggestion that nature was subjected
to decay against its own will, and for the sake of Him who
subjected it. In truth, Paul is here alluding to old myth-
ological stories, elaborations of the old theme of Adam's fall:
just as death was laid as a doom on man in consequence of
his falling a victim to the seduction of Satan, so nature
became doomed to the curse of decay and was thus involved
in the tragic fate of man.
All this sounds very strange. For do we see the curse of
decay at work in nature and do we hear its sighing for
redemption? Does not nature seem to us on the contrary to
be the sphere of inexhaustible vitality? In fact to such an
extent is this the case that if we wish to picture plainly to
ourselves what life is, we think straight away of the vital and
creative forces ever operative in nature's life. To be sure, we
see in nature also the process of coming to be and dying, of
blooming and withering, birth and death. But in nature,
